hints: Look carefully at the functional groups on the left ring and on the right five-membered ring for each steroid.
Check the $\text{C=C}$ bond in the left ring, each $\text{C}$ is already joined to two carbon groups inside fused rings, so cis to trans flipping is impossible.
Compare the carbon skeleton and oxygen count, then think about whether the ring-junction carbons change their chirality when $\text{COCH}_3$ is swapped for $\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
**Spot the oxygen functional groups**

Great start, just read what the O atoms are doing. Both molecules have a $\text{C=O}$ in the six-membered ring on the left, and that is a ketone.

$$\text{ring C=O = ketone (C joined to two other carbons)}$$

**Compare the right-hand side**

Progesterone has an extra $\text{C=O}$ in the $-\text{COCH}_3$ side chain, so that is a second ketone. Testosterone has $-\text{OH}$ directly on the ring, which is a secondary alcohol, but it still keeps the left-ring ketone.

So both molecules contain at least one ketone group.

**Test for geometrical isomerism at C=C**

For $E/Z$ isomerism each $\text{C}$ of $\text{C=C}$ needs two different groups and cis-trans interconversion must be possible. Here the $\text{C=C}$ is locked inside a fused 6-membered ring.

$$\text{ring-locked C=C cannot show geometrical isomerism}$$

**Test molecular formula and chirality**

Progesterone has $\text{C}_{21}\text{H}_{30}\text{O}_2$ with two ketone O atoms, testosterone has $\text{C}_{19}\text{H}_{28}\text{O}_2$ with one ketone O plus one alcohol O. The formulas differ because $\text{COCH}_3$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$.

The steroid ring junctions give the same set of chiral carbons (6 in each). Changing the side-chain group does not create or remove a ring-junction stereocentre, so the chiral count stays the same.

options.A: Half correct, half wrong. Both do contain a ketone, but neither shows geometrical isomerism. The C=C is in a fused ring where the cis arrangement is locked and the trans form cannot exist.
options.B: Both parts fail. Molecular formulas differ (progesterone has the C2 acetyl side chain, testosterone has only OH, so C21 vs C19), and the locked cyclic C=C gives no geometrical isomers.
options.C: The chiral count is indeed the same, but the molecular formulas are not the same. Students choosing this have correctly seen the identical steroid core but missed the difference between COCH3 and OH.
options.D: Correct on both counts. Both keep the left-ring ketone (progesterone has one more), and both have the same number of chiral carbons from the identical fused-ring skeleton.
